Euclidean algorithm for computing the greatest common divisor¶

Given two non-negative integers   a<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi></math>$a$  and   b<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>b</mi></math>$b$ , we have to find their GCD (greatest common divisor), i.e. the largest number which is a divisor of both   a<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi></math>$a$  and   b<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>b</mi></math>$b$ . It's commonly denoted by   gcd(a,b)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">gcd</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$\gcd(a, b)$ . Mathematically it is defined as:

  gcd(a,b)=max{k>0:(k∣a) and (k∣b)}<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">gcd</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">max</mo><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>:</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>∣</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mtext>&nbsp;and&nbsp;</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>∣</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo></math>$$\gcd(a, b) = \max \{k > 0 : (k \mid a) \text{ and } (k \mid b) \}$$ 

(here the symbol "  ∣<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>∣</mo></math>$\mid$ " denotes divisibility, i.e. "  k∣a<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>k</mi><mo>∣</mo><mi>a</mi></math>$k \mid a$ " means "  k<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>k</mi></math>$k$  divides   a<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi></math>$a$ ")

When one of the numbers is zero, while the other is non-zero, their greatest common divisor, by definition, is the second number. When both numbers are zero, their greatest common divisor is undefined (it can be any arbitrarily large number), but it is convenient to define it as zero as well to preserve the associativity of   gcd<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">gcd</mo></math>$\gcd$ . Which gives us a simple rule: if one of the numbers is zero, the greatest common divisor is the other number.

The Euclidean algorithm, discussed below, allows to find the greatest common divisor of two numbers   a<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi></math>$a$  and   b<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>b</mi></math>$b$  in   O(log⁡min(a,b))<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>log</mi><mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo><mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">min</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$O(\log \min(a, b))$ . Since the function is associative, to find the GCD of more than two numbers, we can do   gcd(a,b,c)=gcd(a,gcd(b,c))<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">gcd</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">gcd</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">gcd</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$\gcd(a, b, c) = \gcd(a, \gcd(b, c))$  and so forth.

The algorithm was first described in Euclid's "Elements" (circa 300 BC), but it is possible that the algorithm has even earlier origins.

Algorithm¶

Originally, the Euclidean algorithm was formulated as follows: subtract the smaller number from the larger one until one of the numbers is zero. Indeed, if   g<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>g</mi></math>$g$  divides   a<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi></math>$a$  and   b<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>b</mi></math>$b$ , it also divides   a−b<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi></math>$a-b$ . On the other hand, if   g<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>g</mi></math>$g$  divides   a−b<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi></math>$a-b$  and   b<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>b</mi></math>$b$ , then it also divides   a=b+(a−b)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$a = b + (a-b)$ , which means that the sets of the common divisors of   {a,b}<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo></math>$\{a, b\}$  and   {b,a−b}<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo></math>$\{b,a-b\}$  coincide.

Note that   a<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi></math>$a$  remains the larger number until   b<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>b</mi></math>$b$  is subtracted from it at least   ⌊ab⌋<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow data-mjx-texclass="INNER"><mo data-mjx-texclass="OPEN">⌊</mo><mfrac><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mfrac><mo data-mjx-texclass="CLOSE">⌋</mo></mrow></math>$\left\lfloor\frac{a}{b}\right\rfloor$  times. Therefore, to speed things up,   a−b<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi></math>$a-b$  is substituted with   a−⌊ab⌋b=amodb<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow data-mjx-texclass="INNER"><mo data-mjx-texclass="OPEN">⌊</mo><mfrac><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mfrac><mo data-mjx-texclass="CLOSE">⌋</mo></mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="thickmathspace" rspace="thickmathspace">mod</mo><mi>b</mi></math>$a-\left\lfloor\frac{a}{b}\right\rfloor b = a \bmod b$ . Then the algorithm is formulated in an extremely simple way:

  gcd(a,b)={a,if b=0gcd(b,amodb),otherwise.<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">gcd</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mrow data-mjx-texclass="INNER"><mo data-mjx-texclass="OPEN">{</mo><mtable columnalign="left left" columnspacing="1em" rowspacing=".2em"><mtr><mtd><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo></mtd><mtd><mtext>if&nbsp;</mtext><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">gcd</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="thickmathspace" rspace="thickmathspace">mod</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></mtd><mtd><mtext>otherwise.</mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo data-mjx-texclass="CLOSE" fence="true" stretchy="true" symmetric="true"></mo></mrow></math>$$\gcd(a, b) = \begin{cases}a,&\text{if }b = 0 \\ \gcd(b, a \bmod b),&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$ 

Implementation¶

int gcd (int a, int b) {
    if (b == 0)
        return a;
    else
        return gcd (b, a % b);
}

Using the ternary operator in C++, we can write it as a one-liner.

int gcd (int a, int b) {
    return b ? gcd (b, a % b) : a;
}

And finally, here is a non-recursive implementation:

int gcd (int a, int b) {
    while (b) {
        a %= b;
        swap(a, b);
    }
    return a;
}

Note that since C++17, gcd is implemented as a standard function in C++.

Time Complexity¶

The running time of the algorithm is estimated by Lamé's theorem, which establishes a surprising connection between the Euclidean algorithm and the Fibonacci sequence:

If   a>b≥1<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn></math>$a > b \geq 1$  and   b<Fn<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>b</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>$b < F_n$  for some   n<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>n</mi></math>$n$ , the Euclidean algorithm performs at most   n−2<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></math>$n-2$  recursive calls.

Moreover, it is possible to show that the upper bound of this theorem is optimal. When   a=Fn<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math>$a = F_n$  and   b=Fn−1<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>$b = F_{n-1}$ ,   gcd(a,b)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>g</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$gcd(a, b)$  will perform exactly   n−2<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></math>$n-2$  recursive calls. In other words, consecutive Fibonacci numbers are the worst case input for Euclid's algorithm.

Given that Fibonacci numbers grow exponentially, we get that the Euclidean algorithm works in   O(log⁡min(a,b))<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>log</mi><mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo><mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">min</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$O(\log \min(a, b))$ .

Another way to estimate the complexity is to notice that   amodb<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="thickmathspace" rspace="thickmathspace">mod</mo><mi>b</mi></math>$a \bmod b$  for the case   a≥b<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi><mo>≥</mo><mi>b</mi></math>$a \geq b$  is at least   2<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>2</mn></math>$2$  times smaller than   a<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi></math>$a$ , so the larger number is reduced at least in half on each iteration of the algorithm. Applying this reasoning to the case when we compute the GCD of the set of numbers   a1,…,an≤C<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>…</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mi>C</mi></math>$a_1,\dots,a_n \leq C$ , this also allows us to estimate the total runtime as   O(n+log⁡C)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>log</mi><mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$O(n + \log C)$ , rather than   O(nlog⁡C)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mi>log</mi><mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$O(n \log C)$ , since every non-trivial iteration of the algorithm reduces the current GCD candidate by at least a factor of   2<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>2</mn></math>$2$ .

Least common multiple¶

Calculating the least common multiple (commonly denoted LCM) can be reduced to calculating the GCD with the following simple formula:

  lcm(a,b)=a⋅bgcd(a,b)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"><mtext>lcm</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mrow><mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">gcd</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></math>$$\text{lcm}(a, b) = \frac{a \cdot b}{\gcd(a, b)}$$ 

Thus, LCM can be calculated using the Euclidean algorithm with the same time complexity:

A possible implementation, that cleverly avoids integer overflows by first dividing   a<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi></math>$a$  with the GCD, is given here:

int lcm (int a, int b) {
    return a / gcd(a, b) * b;
}

Binary GCD¶

The Binary GCD algorithm is an optimization to the normal Euclidean algorithm.

The slow part of the normal algorithm are the modulo operations. Modulo operations, although we see them as   O(1)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$O(1)$ , are a lot slower than simpler operations like addition, subtraction or bitwise operations. So it would be better to avoid those.

It turns out, that you can design a fast GCD algorithm that avoids modulo operations. It's based on a few properties:

  • If both numbers are even, then we can factor out a two of both and compute the GCD of the remaining numbers:   gcd(2a,2b)=2gcd(a,b)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">gcd</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">gcd</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$\gcd(2a, 2b) = 2 \gcd(a, b)$ .
  • If one of the numbers is even and the other one is odd, then we can remove the factor 2 from the even one:   gcd(2a,b)=gcd(a,b)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">gcd</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">gcd</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$\gcd(2a, b) = \gcd(a, b)$  if   b<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>b</mi></math>$b$  is odd.
  • If both numbers are odd, then subtracting one number of the other one will not change the GCD:   gcd(a,b)=gcd(b,a−b)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">gcd</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">gcd</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>$\gcd(a, b) = \gcd(b, a-b)$ 

Using only these properties, and some fast bitwise functions from GCC, we can implement a fast version:

int gcd(int a, int b) {
    if (!a || !b)
        return a | b;
    unsigned shift = __builtin_ctz(a | b);
    a >>= __builtin_ctz(a);
    do {
        b >>= __builtin_ctz(b);
        if (a > b)
            swap(a, b);
        b -= a;
    } while (b);
    return a << shift;
}

Notice, that such an optimization is usually not necessary, and most programming languages already have a GCD function in their standard libraries. E.g. C++17 has such a function std::gcd in the numeric header.
